title: Better, Saner Homework Tips, Pt 3: Team Up With Parents and Guardians
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart concludes his three-part homework series by addressing the role of parents and guardians in supporting — or being inadvertently burdened by — homework expectations. He opens with two foundational premises: parents are busy and stressed, and nearly all of them care deeply about their children's success. A warmly empathetic portrait of parental love grounds the practical guidance that follows. The article identifies three firm principles for homework design that respects families: homework should never require parents to teach academic content, expectations should be streamlined and clearly communicated, and students should be explicitly taught every homework type before it is assigned independently. Stuart outlines the two appropriate support roles parents can fill: providing a distraction-free environment and offering listening, encouragement, and coaching toward seeking teacher help. The closing appeal uses a Mr. Rogers-inflected framing to center relational affirmation over performance pressure.
points: Parents are overwhelmed; the teacher's first homework obligation to families is to streamline expectations and communicate them clearly, reducing rather than adding to family cognitive load.
Nearly all parents care deeply about their children — approaching parent relationships from a position of humility about the depth of parental love is the right professional posture.
Homework should never require parents to teach academic content; teachers must explicitly model and teach every homework type before sending it home as an independent task.
Limiting homework to a small number of recurring 'types' reduces the instructional burden of teaching students how to do them and creates predictability that families can plan around.
The two parent support roles that matter most are providing a distraction-free environment and offering emotional encouragement and coaching toward seeking teacher help — not content instruction.
quotes: parents/guardians are busy. Do you know how you feel like you don't have enough time to do all the things you need and want to do in life? That's how all of our students' parents/guardians feel. It's in everyone's best interest to make lives easier by streamlining our homework expectations and communicating them clearly.

just about all parent/guardians I've ever met do care. You know how teaching sometimes makes you feel like the entire weight of your students' long-term flourishing is on your shoulders alone? That's how parents/guardians feel, except there's no off switch for them, including when the school year ends.

Think of how much you love your current students, but multiply that by knowing them since before they were born, watching them first walk and talk, listening to them tell made-up stories, falling in love with their giggle, hearing their dreams for the future take shape and change, watching as their bodies and minds and hearts transform from child to adolescent.

When we think of parents, it needs to be from a humble place — even when we disagree with some of the methods or comments we hear. We have to remind ourselves: they love their child more than I do; they are hugely responsible for the things in their child that I love; they are more frustrated by their child's misbehaviors than I am.

When we send homework home that requires instructional help, it's not fair to students or parents/guardians. As I wrote in Parts 1 and 2, it's my job to explicitly teach my students to do everything I want them to do at home.

the other thing parents can do is listen to and encourage their students. Ask them how things are going. Encourage them for effort wisely applied, for demonstrations of agency and work ethic and focus. Coach them toward seeking help from their teachers. Remind them that their worth isn't in how well they perform in school but rather in who they are.
